sessions.title: Read the product map
concepts: Platform
Databricks combines tools for data processing, analytics, governance, and AI. A workspace is a place to work with these capabilities, subject to your company’s setup.
Storage vs compute
Cloud storage holds the bytes. Compute executes queries and code. Unity Catalog governs registered assets; editors, notebooks, and dashboards are work surfaces.
Your role

A product expert can choose a suitable capability, explain its prerequisites and limits, demonstrate it, and interpret its output. An engineer also implements, tests, deploys, and operates the solution.
sessions.why: You save the team time when you can turn “we need to understand this data” into a specific workflow, deliverable, and access request.
sessions.scenario: A steward asks whether the new platform can find missing data, approve definitions, run checks, and display a scorecard. Route each task to the right capability.
steps: Tour Catalog, SQL, Workspace, Jobs & Pipelines, and Dashboards if they are visible. Menu labels can differ. Record any area that is unavailable.
Choose one permitted table. Identify its three-part name, the tool used to inspect it, and the compute you would need to query values.
Write a short explanation separating platform capabilities from the business decisions your team still owns.
Demonstrate the route from a table to a saved query to a result. If compute is unavailable, make the route map and record the blocker.
sessions.expected: A five-layer map, an availability checklist, and a five-minute demonstration. A visible menu is not evidence that every feature is configured.
sessions.deliverable: Workspace capability map: need, feature, where to find it, access prerequisite, output, limitation, platform contact.
sessions.extension: Create a SQL notebook with a markdown introduction, SELECT 1 AS connectivity_check, and a note identifying the execution context.
sessions.limit: Your end-user sandbox may not include administration, integrations, system-table access, or every AI feature. Learn the boundary without requesting broad admin rights.
sessions.question: How would you tell whether a request needs a new catalog entry, compute, a pipeline, or a business approval?
sessions.answer: Identify what must change: discoverability, execution, data transformation, or an accountable business decision. Then choose the capability that performs that job and list the dependencies.

sessions.title: Understand objects and ownership
concepts: Namespace
catalog.schema.object is an address. A schema here is a namespace, while a table schema also means its column structure.
Objects
A table represents tabular data; an ordinary view is a saved query; a volume governs file access. A folder of files is not automatically a business dataset.
Lifecycle
For managed tables, Databricks manages the storage lifecycle. External-table data is stored in an externally managed location. Storage ownership and business ownership are different responsibilities.
sessions.why: Inventory, retention, deletion, and source integration decisions depend on knowing which type of object you are dealing with.
sessions.scenario: Your team receives a CSV, needs a reusable filtered query, and wants a curated table. Select suitable objects and inspect the lifecycle implications.
steps: In Catalog Explorer, inspect one permitted table and note its type, format, owner, columns, and full name.
Locate a view and, if permitted, inspect its definition. Record the underlying named objects it references.
Inspect an approved volume if available. Explain why its files are different from a registered table’s rows.
Draft an ownership matrix: business steward, table owner, storage/platform owner. Do not test lifecycle behavior by dropping existing objects.
sessions.expected: Three examples with correctly labeled object type, namespace, lifecycle owner, and business steward.
sessions.deliverable: Object register: technical identity, table/view/volume type, managed/external status where applicable, purpose, steward, lifecycle owner.
sessions.extension: In your isolated learning schema, create a view over the synthetic table and compare its definition with the source table. Do not alter shared assets.
sessions.limit: Dropping a managed table and dropping an external table have different storage consequences. View, materialized view, and metric view are also different concepts.
sessions.question: Why can a view be useful even if it does not store a separate copy of its result?
sessions.answer: It gives a reusable named query and a consistent interface. It still depends on underlying objects and compute; it is not automatically a historical snapshot.

sessions.title: Find your identity and execution path
concepts: Discovery vs reading
Seeing metadata is different from reading values. Privilege scope is a common explanation for apparent inventory gaps.
SQL warehouse
A SQL warehouse supplies compute for analytical SQL. A SQL editor stores your query text; it is not the compute itself.
Execution context
The current user, catalog, schema, compute, and object privileges determine where work runs and what it can access.
sessions.why: A precise access request is much more useful than “Databricks is not working.” It lets the vendor or platform owner resolve the actual dependency.
sessions.scenario: Your notebook author can see a table but the intended analyst cannot run the same query. Toggle the missing prerequisites.
steps: Open an approved SQL warehouse or notebook compute. Run the context query in the code shelf.
Use the full name of an approved synthetic table. Query only a small known fixture, not an unrestricted production table.
Capture a successful result or the exact error category, object name, identity, and compute. Keep credentials out of notes.
Write a minimal request for the missing capability. If compute is unavailable, complete the identity and permissions worksheet with the environment owner.
sessions.expected: Documented effective identity, approved compute, namespace, and one successful read—or a specific reproducible blocker.
sessions.deliverable: Sandbox readiness sheet and a reproducible access issue template.
sessions.extension: Parameterize catalog and schema in a notebook or job design. Explain how the run-as identity can differ from the author.
sessions.limit: Serverless is still billable. Inherited privileges, ownership, policies, and compute compatibility can affect access beyond this simplified simulation.
sessions.question: What evidence would distinguish a privilege error from a missing object or unsuitable compute?
sessions.answer: Use the full object name, exact error, effective identity, known visibility scope, and selected compute. Do not conclude that an invisible object does not exist.

sessions.title: Build a defensible inventory
concepts: Scope
An inventory is an observation within a source, identity, object type, filter set, and time—not automatically a complete enterprise census.
Object vs dataset
Multiple files, partitions, and logs can implement one dataset. Agree a grouping rule before comparing S3 objects with registered datasets.
Information schema
Unity Catalog information_schema exposes structured metadata subject to privileges. Its scope differs from a raw S3 inventory or a legacy Hive metastore inventory.
sessions.why: This directly supports your S3/DB registration work. A coverage report becomes useful when its boundaries and reconciliation keys can be defended.
sessions.scenario: The source registry lists 5 intended datasets. Three are registered in this toy catalog, and your role sees only 2. Investigate the gap.
steps: Choose one approved catalog/schema and run a metadata inventory, including full table and column identity.
Save the identity, filters, extraction time, source system, and object types with the result.
Compare against an authorized source list using a documented grouping and identity mapping. Keep unknown matches in a review queue.
Separate “not visible,” “not registered,” “out of scope,” and “confirmed retired.” Do not infer deletion from one missing snapshot.
sessions.expected: In the toy case: source scope 5, registered 3, visible 2 for the limited role. Broader visibility raises visible to 3; it does not register the other 2.
sessions.deliverable: Inventory coverage report with an evidence label and categorized reconciliation gaps.
sessions.extension: Persist dated inventory snapshots in an approved location. Compare two runs by stable identity and classify additions, modifications, and missing observations.
sessions.limit: Metadata extraction is not profiling. Sample-based file-format inference can miss mixed or unstructured content; report the sample boundary.
sessions.question: Why is “2 visible tables / 5 intended datasets” not automatically the final registration-compliance score?
sessions.answer: The numerator and denominator may have different identities, grouping rules, and visibility. Reconcile scope and ownership first, then define the compliance measure under company policy.

sessions.title: Use SQL without losing the business grain
concepts: Grain
Define what a row represents before aggregating: one event, one current loan, one field, or one rule evaluation.
Profiling SQL
COUNT, COUNT DISTINCT, SUM with conditions, and GROUP BY are high-value first tools for governance evidence.
Duplicate vs update
Two rows with the same business key may be legitimate historical updates. Select current state using an explicit order rather than deleting evidence blindly.
sessions.why: Correct grain prevents convincing but misleading scorecards. You can contribute useful work with a small amount of well-understood SQL.
sessions.scenario: The reference fixture has 12 events for 10 loans. Compare an event count with a current-loan count before discussing quality.
steps: Create the synthetic fixture with Field Guide Labs 1–2 in your assigned schema, or inspect its rows in the reference if creation is not allowed.
Run total row count and distinct loan count. Explain the difference before proceeding.
Calculate missing balances and counts by status. Keep observed values distinct from business-approved domains.
Write a sentence defining the grain and denominator beside each result. Re-run it after selecting latest state.
sessions.expected: Raw rows 12; distinct loans 10. The newer L1002 and L1008 events explain the difference. A successful query alone does not establish a correct metric.
sessions.deliverable: Profiling notebook with a small set of defined, reproducible metrics.
sessions.extension: Write ROW_NUMBER over loan_id ordered by event_ts descending and event_id descending. Test a tied timestamp with a deterministic tie-breaker.
sessions.limit: COUNT(column) omits nulls while COUNT(*) counts rows. A join can multiply records when the keys are not unique.
sessions.question: How can two syntactically correct queries answer different business questions over the same table?
sessions.answer: They may evaluate different grains, time windows, filters, joins, or null handling. Define those choices before comparing the outputs.

sessions.title: Connect technical fields to business meaning
concepts: Evidence vs approval
Patterns suggest meanings; source documentation and accountable owner review establish approved mappings.
Stable identity
Match a field using its source/environment/object/column identity or governed stable identifier. Names alone can collide or change.
Attribute authority
Agree which system owns definitions, owners, classifications, and review status before synchronizing metadata between Databricks and Collibra.
sessions.why: Your Collibra skills are immediately valuable here. Treat integrations as governed relationships and review processes, not bulk copying of labels.
sessions.scenario: A field called state could describe a property, borrower, or servicing office. Reveal the source evidence and choose a review state.
steps: Select four synthetic columns and record full technical identity, proposed term, source evidence, owner, and review state.
For state, read the exercise specification: it describes the mortgaged property location. For balance, record ambiguity until confirmed.
Create a mapping review report in the sandbox; use an approved export for Collibra comparison rather than live writeback.
Define conflict handling for two different definitions or owners. Have the accountable steward review the proposal before any synchronization.
sessions.expected: The reference mapping exercise has 2 approved mappings out of 4 targeted fields: 50% targeted coverage. Against 10 total fields, it is 20%.
sessions.deliverable: Term-to-field mapping queue and attribute authority matrix.
sessions.extension: Join mock catalog and glossary exports using explicit keys. Classify matched, missing, conflicting, and ambiguous rows before integration.
sessions.limit: The existence of a Collibra integration does not prove it is configured, entitled, or authorized in your company. Review supported assets and directionality.
sessions.question: Why should an unresolved field remain in the technical inventory?
sessions.answer: Discovery and semantic approval are separate states. Keeping the unresolved field visible supports investigation and prevents falsely inflated completeness.

sessions.title: Create an honest quality scorecard
concepts: Rule, severity, threshold
A rule classifies data; severity defines a response; a threshold decides when to alert. Changing the threshold does not repair data.
Population
State the grain, evaluated population, excluded records, rule version, and evaluation time.
Evidence
A score summarizes named checks. It does not certify business meaning, source reconciliation, or regulatory compliance.
sessions.why: A transparent scorecard can replace repeated ad hoc investigations while giving stewards a clear set of exceptions to resolve.
sessions.scenario: Ten latest loans yield 6 accepted and 4 quarantined under hard rules. Two accepted loans have email warnings. Experiment with severity and alert thresholds.
steps: Run the fixture’s latest-state and validation steps. Preserve a reason for every rejected record.
Build a small dashboard with pass rate, evaluated rows, exceptions by reason, run time, and rule version.
Add the metric definition and warn that technical pass rate is distinct from business or policy compliance.
Check the intended audience and execution identity with the environment owner. Keep the first draft in the approved sandbox audience.
sessions.expected: Baseline v1: 6/10 = 60% accepted; 4 quarantined; 2 accepted records have advisory email issues. Promoting email to a hard rule yields 4/10 = 40%.
sessions.deliverable: A scorecard definition sheet plus a private synthetic dashboard.
sessions.extension: Store a long-form rule_results table with run_id, rule_id, version, evaluated_count, failed_count, scope, and timestamp.
sessions.limit: Dashboard publishing and data execution permissions vary by mode. A green tile does not prove every consumer has appropriate access.
sessions.question: If your manager asks why the score rose, what should you verify before claiming improvement?
sessions.answer: Check whether the population, grain, filters, rule set, severity, threshold, or source changed. Separate an actual reduction in defects from a measurement change.

sessions.title: Deliver your first useful team demo
concepts: Product fluency
Explain what feature you selected, why it fits, what you observed, and what it cannot prove.
Evidence pack
Combine an inventory boundary, profiling output, definition review, and known limitations into one small demonstration.
Adoption
A repeatable artifact with an owner is more useful than a broad tour of menus.
sessions.why: Your first contribution should be small enough to finish and clear enough for someone else to use. This gives you feedback before scaling.
sessions.scenario: Choose what belongs in the first demo. Separate necessary evidence from optional engineering enhancements.
steps: Pick one domain and one agreed question. Use synthetic data until real data access and handling are approved.
Show the source scope, a reproducible query, a score with a denominator, and a mapping requiring review.
Explain at least two limits and identify the next owner decision. Avoid presenting hypothetical time savings as measured outcomes.
Rehearse a five-minute teach-back: problem, feature choice, evidence, limits, next step. Ask a colleague to repeat one result from your notes.
sessions.expected: A reviewer can identify the population, reproduce one number, locate one exception, and state what remains unverified.
sessions.deliverable: First-team-demo brief and feedback log.
sessions.extension: Move the repeatable queries into an ordered notebook, with parameters and a basic count assertion. Keep the schedule off until reviewed.
sessions.limit: A sandbox demonstration is a pilot, not authorization to publish, broaden data access, or change enterprise definitions.
sessions.question: What is the strongest sign that this first demo is useful?
sessions.answer: A teammate can repeat the method, interpret its evidence, and use the result to make the intended next decision—not merely admire the dashboard.

sessions.title: Build trustworthy current-state data
concepts: Medallion layers
Bronze preserves ingested evidence, silver makes typing and grain explicit, and gold serves defined metrics. These are design conventions, not automatic quality levels.
Ordering
For current state, choose the latest event before applying validity rules. Otherwise an old valid row can silently replace a new invalid one.
Reconciliation
For this fixture, latest rows must equal accepted plus quarantined rows, without overlapping membership.
sessions.why: This pattern turns profiling findings into consistent, auditable team data products.
sessions.scenario: L1003 is invalid in current state. A new update can be bad even when an older one was valid. Test the effect of transformation order.
steps: Preserve the raw synthetic events and provenance. Build the latest-state relation using a deterministic key and order.
Parse balance explicitly. Classify missing or invalid values and apply documented state and status domains.
Write accepted and quarantine outputs with the same evaluation version. Aggregate only the intended accepted population.
Reconcile counts and manually inspect representative failures. Explain the tradeoff of excluding invalid latest records from gold.
sessions.expected: 12 raw events → 10 latest loans → 6 accepted + 4 quarantine. Accepted balance totals 1,289,000, including a paid loan with zero balance.
sessions.deliverable: Bronze/silver/gold data contract and quarantine reason report.
sessions.extension: Implement the same logic using PySpark DataFrames, then compare row membership and aggregates against SQL.
sessions.limit: The chosen acceptance rules are fictional teaching rules, not your company’s lending or governance policy.
sessions.question: What is dangerous about dropping invalid records before choosing the newest row?
sessions.answer: It can resurrect stale state. Decide recency first, then handle a failing current record explicitly and transparently.

sessions.title: Choose the right quality control
concepts: Validation vs monitoring
Validation evaluates an explicit rule at a point in processing. Monitoring observes behavior over time. These answer different questions.
Expectations
Pipeline expectations can retain invalid rows with metrics, drop them, or fail the affected update. Quarantine requires an explicit design.
Native monitoring
Databricks data quality monitoring includes anomaly detection for freshness/completeness patterns and table profiling. Availability, permissions, and compute costs must be checked.
sessions.why: Your team needs controls tied to a risk and response, not a growing collection of unowned scores.
sessions.scenario: A batch has 10 rows and 4 fail a rule. Choose warn, drop, fail, or an explicit quarantine design and inspect the consequences.
steps: Choose one business-reviewed rule and state what happens on failure. Separate advisory warnings from acceptance gates.
Use the expectations lab if pipeline access exists. Otherwise reproduce the classifications with SQL and document the equivalent intended behavior.
Compare retained, excluded, failed-update, and quarantine outcomes. Record whether a metric was actually available for the failed run.
Assess native profiling/anomaly monitoring with the owner if available. Define who investigates each alert and what evidence closes it.
sessions.expected: Warn retains 10 rows; drop retains 6; fail prevents a successful affected update. Explicit quarantine produces 6 accepted + 4 investigated records in this model.
sessions.deliverable: Rule registry: condition, grain, severity, action, owner, version, exception handling, and evidence source.
sessions.extension: Implement expectations and inspect the event log in your permitted pipeline. Compare the SQL fallback outputs rather than assuming identical operational behavior.
sessions.limit: Monitoring is not an ingestion gate. Failed expectations can have different metric availability, and quarantine is not created simply by choosing drop.
sessions.question: When is a hard failure appropriate instead of retaining a warning?
sessions.answer: When the agreed contract requires stopping the affected output and an owner can diagnose and recover it. The response should match business risk and operational recovery needs.

sessions.title: Choose ingestion or federation
concepts: Ingestion
Ingestion moves data into a target for processing. A connector choice depends on source support, incremental behavior, freshness, and operations.
Federation
Query federation queries a supported external database; catalog federation can access external catalog tables through supported storage paths. They have different execution paths.
Tradeoff
Copying introduces freshness and lifecycle duties. Querying in place preserves a dependency on the source and its supported behavior.
sessions.why: You can guide source onboarding by distinguishing “register it,” “read it,” and “copy it” before engineering starts.
sessions.scenario: You need a one-off operational lookup, a recurring high-volume report, or incremental S3 ingestion. Compare the dependency and freshness tradeoffs.
steps: For one authorized source, document format, volume, update pattern, latency need, network path, owner, and intended use.
Compare available federation, managed connector, and file ingestion options with the platform owner. Check the specific connector’s support and release state.
Choose a small synthetic proof of concept. If connectivity is not available, produce the decision record without creating credentials or connections.
Write failure and reconciliation requirements: source unavailable, late updates, deletions, schema changes, and replay.
sessions.expected: A decision that names the execution path, data movement, freshness target, source load, owner dependencies, and unverified assumptions.
sessions.deliverable: Source onboarding decision record.
sessions.extension: Run the reference volume/COPY INTO or Auto Loader lab in an approved location. Do not treat file-level tracking as business-key deduplication.
sessions.limit: Do not assume every source, cloud, or region supports the same connector. Federation is not universal ingestion or automatic enterprise discovery.
sessions.question: Why might querying in place be a poor default for every recurring workload?
sessions.answer: The source remains a runtime dependency and can bear query load. Assess scale, latency, supported pushdown, and operational requirements before choosing it.

sessions.title: Automate evidence with Jobs
concepts: Task graph
Jobs coordinate tasks, dependencies, triggers, and execution settings. A successful upstream task should establish the inputs needed downstream.
Run identity
An automated run may use permissions different from the notebook author’s.
Idempotency
Retries must not create duplicate results or external side effects. Stable keys and deliberate write semantics are essential.
sessions.why: Scheduled inventory and quality evidence can replace repeated manual execution, but only if failures are understandable and recoverable.
sessions.scenario: A run writes a ticket then fails. Repeated retries can create duplicate tickets unless the receiver recognizes the same business key.
steps: Create a small job in your permitted workspace with tasks for synthetic preparation, validation, and metrics publication.
Set task dependencies explicitly and inspect the intended run-as identity. Keep schedules disabled until manual runs are reviewed.
Inject a deterministic quality failure. Show that retrying unchanged invalid input does not fix the defect.
Repeat a successful run and reconcile outputs. Simulate external notifications rather than sending real messages during practice.
sessions.expected: A repeat run preserves intended results; a failed check has a diagnosable owner and recovery step; dependent work does not silently consume an invalid update.
sessions.deliverable: Job operating guide with dependencies, identity, retry conditions, idempotency keys, and recovery steps.
sessions.extension: Add a run ledger and assertion task. Design key uniqueness for each side effect and test a partially completed run.
sessions.limit: Automatic retries are appropriate for some transient failures, not an unlimited response to deterministic data defects. Production schedules and notifications need the company’s process.
sessions.question: What should a retry change when the failure was caused by the input violating a rule?
sessions.answer: Nothing will improve without correcting or explicitly handling the cause. Diagnose, preserve evidence, and rerun under the agreed recovery procedure.

sessions.title: Test governance controls and lineage
concepts: Classification vs enforcement
Tags describe data; applicable privileges and policies enforce access. ABAC uses attributes in configured policies.
Effective access
Test what the intended identity can discover and read, including any applicable row filters or column masks.
Observed lineage
Captured paths support impact analysis but do not establish complete coverage of external consumers.
sessions.why: This produces security and dependency evidence for releases without assuming that descriptive catalog metadata protects data.
sessions.scenario: Turn a classification label, mask, and privilege on or off. Then decide what a missing lineage edge can and cannot prove.
steps: Use only the isolated synthetic table from the masking lab and only privileges you already own or are approved to use.
Compare an ordinary identity with an authorized policy exception using the approved testing process. If no second identity is available, record the untested branch.
Inspect named-table lineage where visible. Record external consumers or paths separately from captured edges.
Create a control test record with identity, object, policy version, expected result, observed result, time, and unresolved coverage.
sessions.expected: A tag alone does not change the simulated value. An applicable mask does; missing read prerequisites deny access. Untested identities remain explicitly unverified.
sessions.deliverable: Access test matrix and lineage coverage note.
sessions.extension: Design reusable masking or ABAC policy tests with your security/platform owner. Do not broaden permissions to make a test convenient.
sessions.limit: Policies, ownership, inherited grants, group membership, compute support, and dashboard/job execution mode can affect real results. This is not a complete authorization engine.
sessions.question: What additional evidence is needed before deleting a table with no visible downstream lineage?
sessions.answer: Confirm capture and visibility scope, usage, external extracts, and owner knowledge. No observed edge does not prove there are no consumers.

sessions.title: Reconcile Collibra without overwriting trust
concepts: Reconciliation
Compare identities and governed attributes before deciding whether metadata should change.
Conflict handling
A difference can reflect stale sync, a rename, wrong matching, or a real change. It is not always safe to overwrite one side.
Directionality
Document the authority and permitted synchronization direction for each attribute. Business approval and technical extraction are separate events.
sessions.why: A reviewable diff is often a stronger first team contribution than attempting fully automatic catalog synchronization.
sessions.scenario: Five synthetic assets include a match, a rename, an unregistered asset, a conflicting definition, and an out-of-scope observation.
steps: Use approved exports or the mock datasets from the reference lab. Include stable IDs, environment, names, timestamps, and review status.
Join using the agreed identity mapping. Separate ambiguous or unmatched identities before comparing descriptive values.
Classify differences and assign review actions. Preserve both old and proposed values and the evidence for any rename.
Have the relevant steward review the queue. Keep live writeback disabled until scope, attribute authority, conflict rules, and rollback are approved.
sessions.expected: Each difference is categorized and reviewable. A matching display name does not override an ID mismatch or an unapproved definition.
sessions.deliverable: Catalog reconciliation report: asset identity, difference class, authoritative source, old/new values, evidence, owner, proposed action.
sessions.extension: Build deterministic diff keys and idempotent imports in a mock pipeline. Preserve manual-review and approval states across reruns.
sessions.limit: Connector support, lineage ingestion, metadata extraction, and outbound synchronization are distinct capabilities. Your deployment and entitlement determine what is available.
sessions.question: Why is “last writer wins” risky for business definitions?
sessions.answer: An extraction timestamp is not proof of authority or approval. A newer technical comment may be less authoritative than an approved stewardship decision.

sessions.title: Model metrics people can trust
concepts: Semantic definition
A business metric needs a formula, population, grain, dimensions, time logic, and treatment of missing or excluded data.
Metric views
Unity Catalog metric views centralize measure definitions separately from grouping dimensions for supported consumers.
Ratio behavior
A ratio of totals and an unweighted average of subgroup percentages often differ. The correct choice follows the business definition.
sessions.why: Shared definitions reduce disagreements between dashboards and make business-facing analysis more reproducible.
sessions.scenario: One group passes 9 of 10 checks; another passes 1 of 90. Compare the overall pass rate with the average of the two percentages.
steps: Write a definition for one governance measure, such as approved mapping coverage over targeted fields.
Build a small SQL result using the two-group fixture in the code shelf. Compare ratio of totals with average of group rates.
If metric views are available, review how a supported semantic object would encode the approved measure. Otherwise create a definition sheet and ordinary query.
Compare the dashboard result against the SQL baseline and verify intended grouping, filtering, and time scope.
sessions.expected: Overall pass rate is (9+1)/(10+90)=10%. The unweighted mean of 90% and about 1.11% is about 45.56%; it answers a different question.
sessions.deliverable: Metric definition contract and a reconciled scorecard query.
sessions.extension: Build a metric view in the approved environment using the current syntax and supported runtime, then validate results across dimensions.
sessions.limit: Semantic objects do not approve meaning. Wrong joins, filters, and denominator definitions can still produce misleading metrics.
sessions.question: When could an unweighted average of group percentages be intentional?
sessions.answer: When the agreed metric gives each group equal weight regardless of size. Label that definition explicitly instead of presenting it as the record-level pass rate.

sessions.title: Measure cost and performance before scaling
concepts: Scan work
Returned rows and processed data are different. LIMIT is not a general guarantee of a cheap scan.
Evidence
Use query profile/history and available operational evidence to find scans, joins, shuffles, spill, or repeated work.
Attribution
Frequency, data volume, compute, and maintenance all influence usage. Cost estimates need actual billing context and rates.
sessions.why: A governance check that is useful on one table can become expensive when run across many tables every hour.
sessions.scenario: Estimate relative scan work by changing frequency, number of tables, and fraction scanned. No dollar price is assumed.
steps: Choose one small approved query and record its duration and available scan metrics. Avoid benchmarking production-scale copies.
Apply a meaningful filter or reduce unnecessary columns where appropriate, then compare equivalent results and observed work.
Document schedule frequency and table coverage for a proposed monitoring job. Use an aggregate snapshot where it meets the need.
If system billing/query data is unavailable, request a scoped owner-provided summary. Do not invent savings or rates.
sessions.expected: A baseline-and-change comparison with unchanged business result, observed performance evidence, and explicit cost-estimate assumptions.
sessions.deliverable: Cost-aware monitoring proposal and a query tuning evidence note.
sessions.extension: Inspect EXPLAIN and query profile for a measured bottleneck. Evaluate layout/optimization choices with the table owner rather than applying every tuning feature.
sessions.limit: The simulator models relative scan volume only. Real costs include compute behavior, caching, storage, network, services, and contracted pricing.
sessions.question: Why can a faster individual query still produce a larger monthly bill?
sessions.answer: It may run much more often, use more costly resources, or cover more data and services. Compare the whole workload and actual usage.

sessions.title: Design incremental ingestion and safe replay
concepts: State
Incremental workloads track what they processed. The checkpoint and target data have related but distinct lifecycles.
File identity vs business key
Tracking a processed file does not prevent the same business event from appearing in a different file.
Replay
Recovery can reread input. The downstream write design determines whether that creates duplicates or converges to the intended result.
sessions.why: Reliable daily governance evidence depends on handling reruns, late arrivals, and duplicated input without silently inflating reports.
sessions.scenario: The source contains 2 files with 3 business events, one repeated across files. A later file contains one update. Simulate reruns and checkpoint reset.
steps: Use the synthetic volume/Auto Loader lab with a unique checkpoint in an approved learning location.
Run once, rerun unchanged input, then add a new file. Record file arrivals separately from distinct business keys.
Design business-key deduplication or merge behavior downstream. Test a repeated event under a new filename.
Describe a checkpoint-loss recovery plan with the owner. Use the simulator for resets; do not reset a shared checkpoint as an experiment.
sessions.expected: The simulator ingests each file once with preserved state, yet business duplicates still require downstream logic. Resetting state can replay files.
sessions.deliverable: Incremental ingestion contract and replay test record.
sessions.extension: Implement deterministic upserts, rescued-data handling, and schema evolution behavior. Test out-of-order and duplicate events with fixed expected outcomes.
sessions.limit: The simulator is a simplified state model, not a claim about all exactly-once guarantees. Real behavior depends on source, sink, checkpoint, query, and retention.
sessions.question: Why are both ingestion state and business-key logic necessary?
sessions.answer: They solve different duplicate problems: repeated processing of a source unit and repeated representation of a business event or entity.

sessions.title: Turn notebooks into governed releases
concepts: Versioned artifacts
Code, resource configuration, rule versions, and environment parameters must be reviewable together.
Bundles and automation
Declarative Automation Bundles support defining and deploying Databricks resources as code. Older materials may call them Asset Bundles.
Environment boundaries
A dev result does not prove target permissions, data dependencies, secrets, or runtime behavior. Revalidate in the intended environment.
sessions.why: You can improve P2P release evidence even before you own deployment infrastructure.
sessions.scenario: Build a release pack and identify missing gates. A notebook that ran once has not yet demonstrated safe promotion.
steps: Take the synthetic job and record its code version, inputs, rule versions, environment parameters, and run identity.
List checks for the target environment: object names, grants, compute, dependencies, expected counts, and recovery behavior.
Prepare a reviewable release record and a rollback/recovery exercise on an isolated copy. Follow your company’s actual P2P gates.
If you have deployment tooling access, inspect a bundle in a development target with the owner. Do not point a training command at production.
sessions.expected: A reviewer can identify the exact intended change, reproduce validation, and explain how an unsuccessful rollout will be handled.
sessions.deliverable: Release evidence pack with target-specific validation and an owner-approved recovery path.
sessions.extension: Define a small development-only bundle, validate configuration, and test deployment in the permitted dev target using the current CLI and team review process.
sessions.limit: A source-code rollback does not automatically undo data writes or external side effects. Recovery must address each affected state.
sessions.question: What can go wrong if the only promoted artifact is a copied notebook?
sessions.answer: Its target object names, identity, libraries, compute, dependencies, and schedules can differ from the test environment, and there may be no reproducible version or recovery path.

sessions.title: Investigate freshness and incident signals
concepts: Freshness vs completeness
A recently updated table can still be missing records. A normal row count can still contain invalid business values.
Signals vs guarantees
Statistical monitoring detects deviations from learned or chosen baselines. It does not establish every business rule.
Observability
Run history, event logs, system tables, quality outputs, and source reconciliation provide complementary evidence with distinct access and retention boundaries.
sessions.why: A useful operational report explains what broke, which consumers may be affected, and who should act.
sessions.scenario: Change arrival delay, row count, and failed-rule count. See why one green signal cannot establish overall health.
steps: Define a freshness requirement and an expected population for one synthetic dataset, with its owner and investigation window.
Compare the latest successful processing time, source arrival time, counts, and quality outcomes. Keep event time and processing time distinct.
Inspect native monitoring or permitted operational tables if available. Record which signals are missing or delayed.
Draft an incident timeline and response route. Use mock recipients; do not send training alerts to real teams.
sessions.expected: An incident note can distinguish late ingestion, incomplete population, invalid content, and missing evidence. Unknown is a valid status.
sessions.deliverable: Data health triage board and incident runbook.
sessions.extension: Combine run-ledger and quality-results tables by stable run and dataset identity. Design duplicate suppression and closure criteria for alerts.
sessions.limit: System-table availability, regional scope, latency, and retention vary by table and deployment. Platform health is not the same as business validity.
sessions.question: Can a fresh table still be unsuitable for a business report?
sessions.answer: Yes. It may be incomplete, fail a rule, have wrong semantics, or include a changed population. Use several independent signals and explain their limits.

sessions.title: Design recovery around data lifecycle
concepts: History
Delta history and time travel help inspect previous table states when required metadata and files remain available.
Recovery objectives
RPO describes acceptable data loss; RTO describes acceptable recovery time. Both must be agreed for the workload.
Lifecycle
Retention, source replay, downstream writes, and external side effects affect what recovery is actually possible.
sessions.why: Your team should know what its evidence and release process can recover before relying on it for an important decision.
sessions.scenario: Choose whether the needed historical files exist and whether source replay is available. Compare table restoration with full workflow recovery.
steps: On the isolated copy from Lab 7, inspect table history and available prior versions. Record the version used for a comparison.
Describe the data changes, code changes, derived outputs, and side effects that a recovery would need to address.
Ask the platform owner for applicable retention and backup/replay arrangements. Do not alter shared retention or run VACUUM as practice.
Write and review a tabletop recovery plan. Test only the approved isolated scenario, then record observed time and remaining gaps.
sessions.expected: A recovery decision distinguishes available table history, source replay, recomputation, and external effects. It does not equate time travel with a full backup.
sessions.deliverable: Recovery coverage matrix with objectives, dependencies, test evidence, and owners.
sessions.extension: Build a reproducible reprocessing job on the synthetic fixture. Prove deterministic outputs and reconcile any rerun side effects.
sessions.limit: Historical versions are not indefinitely available. A restored source does not automatically repair all derived tables or external consumers.
sessions.question: Why is “we can roll back the table” an incomplete recovery plan?
sessions.answer: The incident may also affect jobs, downstream datasets, policies, published reports, or external actions. Each state needs a recovery path and verification.

sessions.title: Govern reusable semantics and AI answers
concepts: Semantic context
Definitions, examples, dimensions, and approved metric logic help people and AI interpret data consistently.
Evaluation
Judge an AI-assisted answer against a known question, approved query, expected result, and permission context.
Human authority
Generated descriptions and classifications are proposals until reviewed under your governance process.
sessions.why: The high-value contribution is a trustworthy business question set and semantic evidence, not simply enabling an AI interface.
sessions.scenario: An AI answer says “pass rate is 45.56%.” Inspect its denominator and compare with the approved record-level rate of 10%.
steps: Choose three non-sensitive business questions with approved definitions and synthetic expected results.
Where an approved AI/BI or assistance feature is available, compare its query and answer with your baseline. Otherwise review the supplied hypothetical answer.
Classify errors: wrong grain, wrong filter, unsupported definition, incomplete data, or inappropriate access.
Create a review log and a semantic improvement proposal. Measure correctness on the question set after changing definitions or examples.
sessions.expected: Each answer is accepted, rejected, or unresolved using evidence. A fluent explanation and syntactically valid SQL are not sufficient.
sessions.deliverable: AI answer evaluation pack with questions, approved logic, expected results, identity, observed output, and review decisions.
sessions.extension: Automate comparison of approved benchmark queries where appropriate and include regression cases for ambiguous terms and small denominators.
sessions.limit: AI tools, models, entitlements, and data access vary. Do not place sensitive content in an unapproved tool or treat a model suggestion as a stewardship decision.
sessions.question: What evidence makes an AI-generated metric answer trustworthy for a specific use?
sessions.answer: Its meaning, population, query, result, freshness, and access context agree with the approved benchmark and the intended business question.

sessions.title: Know when the wider platform matters
concepts: Sharing and collaboration
Sharing and clean-room capabilities serve controlled collaboration needs. They require appropriate configuration and a defined recipient or collaboration model.
ML and applications
MLflow, model/AI workflows, Databricks Apps, and operational database capabilities address needs beyond routine governance reporting.
Prioritization
A product expert knows enough to recognize a fit, ask the right dependency questions, and involve a specialist. Depth should follow an actual use case.
sessions.why: You can become the team’s useful product navigator without learning every feature to implementation depth at once.
sessions.scenario: Route four requests: share an approved dataset, evaluate a model, build a business app, or produce a daily inventory report.
steps: Review the platform capability map and identify which features your workspace exposes. Record “not verified” where configuration is unknown.
For one credible team request, compare its need with sharing, AI/ML, Apps, operational data, or standard SQL/Jobs.
Write the prerequisites, data boundary, owner/specialist, likely output, and evidence needed to decide whether a proof of concept is worthwhile.
Choose what to defer. Do not initiate integrations, share datasets, or create paid services merely to complete this session.
sessions.expected: A feature-fit matrix with one justified exploration and explicit deferrals tied to current team needs.
sessions.deliverable: Product capability decision matrix and specialist handoff brief.
sessions.extension: Choose one approved extension after the core pilot is working. Use the official tutorial and an isolated synthetic dataset to validate fit.
sessions.limit: Names, availability, release states, and entitlements evolve. Broad awareness does not equal operational expertise in every subsystem.
sessions.question: When is saying “we do not need that feature yet” the expert answer?
sessions.answer: When a simpler supported workflow meets the need and the additional feature adds cost, permissions, or operational dependencies without justified benefit.

sessions.title: Choose and defend an implementation proposal
concepts: Value
Prioritize a recurring team problem with a named consumer and measurable baseline. A subjective priority score helps compare ideas but does not prove ROI.
Feasibility
Consider data readiness, access, feature availability, integration dependencies, and who will own the result after the pilot.
Acceptance
Define success using reproducibility, correctness, coverage, usability, and operating effort—not just a delivered dashboard.
sessions.why: Your strongest early reputation comes from delivering a small reliable improvement and showing its measured effect.
sessions.scenario: Adjust value, feasibility, and effort for three candidate projects. Compare the recommendation and challenge its assumptions.
steps: Pick one of the three recommended projects and document a baseline from the team’s actual workflow.
Define the smallest approved dataset scope, consumer, owner, dependencies, and acceptance checks.
Implement the sandbox pilot and compare its evidence with the existing method. Measure effort saved only after observing it.
Prepare an adoption proposal with known limits and operating responsibilities. Route production changes through the company’s approval process.
sessions.expected: A one-page proposal with a measurable baseline, a narrow scope, acceptance gates, costs/dependencies, and an accountable operating owner.
sessions.deliverable: Team pilot proposal and measured before/after evidence.
sessions.extension: Turn the successful pilot into versioned queries, a reviewed job, explicit permissions, and a small recovery runbook.
sessions.limit: The ranking tool uses your subjective inputs, not verified financial value. Production rollout may require platform, security, source, and steward participation.
sessions.question: What would make you stop or reshape the pilot?
sessions.answer: Missing authority to use the data, irreconcilable definitions, unacceptable runtime cost, no owner, or evidence that the proposed result does not improve the intended workflow.

sessions.title: Prove product mastery and start exam preparation
concepts: Demonstration
Show a feature working, explain its data and permission assumptions, and identify when another approach is better.
Engineering transfer
Build, test, rerun, diagnose, promote, and recover a small pipeline. These skills complement product knowledge.
Certification
The Data Engineer Associate exam targets foundational engineering. Certification preparation should follow the current official blueprint and hands-on gap assessment.
sessions.why: A capstone and a teach-back make your progress visible. The certificate can then validate part of the skill set instead of substituting for it.
sessions.scenario: Review your evidence across product decisions, workspace demonstrations, failure handling, and recovery. Identify gaps before booking.
steps: Complete the three-project evidence pack or one integrated capstone that covers their core outputs.
Demonstrate a new scenario: a missing privilege, late update, rule failure, metadata conflict, or changed denominator. Predict the outcome first.
Give a ten-minute product teach-back and a separate engineering walkthrough. Have a reviewer challenge assumptions and record corrections.
Read the current official Associate exam guide, map gaps, and plan targeted study. Treat Professional-level certification as a later milestone after deeper operating experience.
sessions.expected: You can explain and demonstrate the selected scope without a script, diagnose an unfamiliar variation, and state the remaining unverified areas.
sessions.deliverable: Product mastery portfolio, engineering gap list, and a certification study decision.
sessions.extension: Rebuild the capstone with a reproducible deployment workflow and automated regression cases. Practice SQL and PySpark behaviors required by the current exam guide.
sessions.limit: Course completion or a sandbox capstone does not make you an expert in every Databricks product. Expertise grows through varied real workloads, incidents, and review.
sessions.question: What is a better readiness measure than finishing every session quickly?
sessions.answer: Independent performance on new cases: correct explanations, reproducible outputs, appropriate feature choices, and safe diagnosis and recovery within the agreed scope.
